govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AutopsyJFKMorga:
Dr. Russell H. Morgan, a leading radiologist, was among the experts who examined the Kennedy autopsy X-ray films for the government. This Washington Post article reports his explanation of those films and the question of whether they should be released to the public.

The autopsy photographs and X-rays were held under tight restriction, which made expert commentary like Morgan's one of the few public windows on them. He addressed what the films showed and why access to them was limited. The article is press coverage of the medical evidence fight, preserved from the newspaper's pages for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BroshearsRayRev:
Stephen Jaffe wrote this article on August 5, 1968, during Jim Garrison's New Orleans investigation. It reports Reverend Raymond Broshears' account of what David Ferrie's former roommate said Ferrie had confessed, a story aired on the Tempo I television show in Los Angeles, hosted by Stan Bohrman.

Ferrie, the eccentric pilot Garrison tied to Oswald, had died in 1967, so claims about his confessions could only travel secondhand, through roommates and ministers on talk shows. Broshears became a recurring witness in the Garrison orbit, and researchers have argued over his reliability ever since. The article preserves one of the era's strangest claims in its original form.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Hardin-AshmoreR:
An FBI teletype dated May 30, 1968 went to the Director and to field offices in Memphis, Atlanta, San Diego, Birmingham, and Springfield. Its subject was the investigation of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, then seven weeks old. The manhunt and its leads crossed the whole country, and the wire tied the offices together.

Teletypes set the pace of a national investigation before computers did. One message could task five cities at once, and this one did. The wire preserves the Bureau coordinating the King case in real time, office by office.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LoveladyWilliam: On March 2, 1964, FBI agents interviewed Billy Nolan Lovelady, and the interview was written up on the bureau's standard FD-302 form. Lovelady worked at the Texas School Book Depository in Dallas, and his statements about November 22, 1963 formed part of the Oswald inquiry. The file gives the form, the date, and the man interviewed, but no summary of what he said on this occasion.
